vignette: John, a 42-year-old ship captain from the East Coast, has been struggling with intense anxiety and intrusive memories since he survived a major oil spill at sea. The event occurred six months ago while he was navigating his vessel through rough waters off the coast of Newfoundland. Despite all efforts to avoid it, the collision between two cargo ships triggered an uncontrolled release of thousands of gallons of crude oil into the ocean. John vividly recalls the chaos and desperation that ensued after the accident. He had been on watch when the alarm sounded; the sudden impact shook his vessel violently, and within minutes, the oily black slick began to spread across the water's surface like a thick stain. As he coordinated with the crew to secure the ship and ensure everyone’s safety, John witnessed the devastating impact of the spill on marine life and the surrounding ecosystem. The haunting images of oil-coated seabirds floundering in the water have stayed with him ever since. In the days following the disaster, John felt a sense of relief that no one had been seriously injured. However, over time, he began to experience disturbing flashbacks during quiet moments when his mind would wander back to that fateful night. He often finds himself replaying the events in vivid detail and is plagued by nightmares where he relives the shock and helplessness of the moment. At home, John’s wife notices changes in him as well. He has become increasingly irritable and short-tempered, frequently snapping at her over minor issues. Even when they go out to dinner or watch a movie together, he tends to feel on edge, constantly scanning the environment for potential threats. This hypervigilance has made it difficult for John to relax and enjoy simple pleasures that once brought him joy. His occupation as a ship captain has also been affected by his PTSD symptoms. At work, John often feels overwhelmed by tasks that used to be routine. He experiences intense anxiety when navigating through similar waters where the spill occurred, feeling an overwhelming sense of dread at every turn. His concentration has become sporadic; he finds himself frequently distracted and struggling to focus on detailed instructions or safety protocols. During his sessions with me, John describes a persistent sense of guilt over what happened that night. He wonders if there was something more he could have done to prevent the disaster. These thoughts contribute to his ongoing feelings of shame and self-blame. Even though colleagues and superiors have assured him that accidents like this are unpredictable and beyond anyone’s control, John still grapples with a deep sense of responsibility for the environmental damage caused. John also avoids activities related to his trauma, such as watching news reports about oil spills or reading articles about their ecological impact. He has stopped going to the beach where he used to take long walks during downtime, feeling the sand beneath his feet triggers memories of that night. This avoidance extends to social gatherings; John often makes excuses to skip family get-togethers and avoids conversations centered around maritime events. Despite these challenges, John is committed to managing his symptoms and seeks support through therapy sessions. He acknowledges the importance of addressing his PTSD but struggles with balancing this need for care with the demands of his job. John hopes that by sharing his experiences and working through them, he can regain a sense of control over his life and find some peace amidst the ongoing trauma. His story highlights the profound impact of man-made disasters on individuals, illustrating how deeply embedded memories and emotions can affect one's daily functioning and relationships. Through our sessions, we explore coping strategies and techniques to help John navigate through these challenging times, though he continues to grapple with the lingering effects of that fateful night at sea.
